final_proof:
Let
\[
C(I)=\{f:I\to\mathbb R:f\text{ is continuous}\}.
\]
For \(f,g\in C(I)\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x),\qquad (\lambda\cdot f)(x)=\lambda f(x)
\quad(x\in I).
\]

First, these operations are closed on \(C(I)\). If \(f,g\) are continuous on \(I\), then their sum \(f+g\) is continuous on \(I\). If \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(f\) is continuous on \(I\), then \(\lambda f\) is continuous on \(I\). Hence pointwise addition maps \(C(I)\times C(I)\) into \(C(I)\), while pointwise scalar multiplication maps \(\mathbb R\times C(I)\) into \(C(I)\).

Define \(0_C:I\to\mathbb R\) by \(0_C(x)=0\) for every \(x\in I\). This constant function is continuous, so \(0_C\in C(I)\). For \(f\in C(I)\), define \(-f:I\to\mathbb R\) by \((-f)(x)=-f(x)\). This function is continuous because it is the scalar multiple \((-1)f\), so \(-f\in C(I)\).

It remains to verify the vector-space identities. Let \(f,g,h\in C(I)\), let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), and let \(x\in I\). The corresponding identities in \(\mathbb R\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
((f+g)+h)(x)
 &= (f(x)+g(x))+h(x) \\
 &= f(x)+(g(x)+h(x))
  = (f+(g+h))(x),\\
(f+g)(x)
 &=f(x)+g(x)=g(x)+f(x)=(g+f)(x),\\
(f+0_C)(x)
 &=f(x)+0=f(x),\\
(f+(-f))(x)
 &=f(x)-f(x)=0=0_C(x),\\
(\alpha\cdot(f+g))(x)
 &=\alpha(f(x)+g(x))\\
 &=\alpha f(x)+\alpha g(x)
  =((\alpha\cdot f)+(\alpha\cdot g))(x),\\
((\alpha+\beta)\cdot f)(x)
 &=(\alpha+\beta)f(x)\\
 &=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(x)
  =((\alpha\cdot f)+(\beta\cdot f))(x),\\
((\alpha\beta)\cdot f)(x)
 &=(\alpha\beta)f(x)
  =\alpha(\beta f(x))
  =(\alpha\cdot(\beta\cdot f))(x),\\
(1\cdot f)(x)&=1f(x)=f(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because functions with the same domain are equal whenever their values agree at every point of that domain, these pointwise equalities prove, respectively, associativity and commutativity of addition, the additive-identity and additive-inverse laws, both distributive laws, compatibility of scalar multiplication with multiplication in \(\mathbb R\), and the scalar-identity law. Together with closure, these are all the vector-space axioms over \(\mathbb R\). Therefore \((C(I),+,\cdot)\) is a real vector space.
